Also shows the capacity factor, avoided grid CO₂ emissions, and rough everyday equivalences. Pick a city preset for an indicative peak-sun-hours figure or enter your own. Pure arithmetic — a planning sanity check, not a substitute for a site survey. Everything runs locally in your browser.

tools.name: Body Surface Area (BSA) Calculator
tools.description: Compute body surface area in m² from height and weight using four standard clinical formulas — Mosteller (the common default), Du Bois & Du Bois, Haycock and Boyd. BSA is used alongside BMI for indexing cardiac output, renal clearance and many drug doses. Height and weight accept metric or imperial, and the worked Mosteller formula is shown. Pure arithmetic, in your browser.

tools.name: Simple Syrup Calculator
tools.description: Work out how much sugar and water to weigh out for a batch of simple syrup at any ratio by weight. Enter the target syrup mass and the sugar:water ratio (1:1 standard, 2:1 rich, 3:1 gomme) and get grams of sugar and water, the resulting °Brix (sugar by mass), and approximate volumes. Weighing by mass is accurate since sugar volume isn't additive with water. Pure arithmetic, in your browser.

tools.name: Reverberation Time (RT60) Calculator
tools.description: Estimate a room's reverberation time (RT60 — seconds for sound to decay 60 dB) from its volume and the absorption of its surfaces, using both the Sabine and Eyring formulas. Add each surface with its area and an absorption coefficient (common materials preset), and get total absorption, average α, both RT60 values, and guidance on whether the room suits speech, music or neither. Pure arithmetic, in your browser.

tools.name: Air Density Calculator
tools.description: Compute the density of moist air in kg/m³ from temperature, pressure and relative humidity using the ideal-gas mixture formula, plus the derived pressure and density altitude and the difference from the ICAO standard atmosphere (1.225 kg/m³ at 15 °C, 1013.25 hPa). Enter station pressure or switch to altitude mode. Useful for engine tuning, drone and aircraft performance, HVAC, ballistics and cycling aerodynamics. Pure arithmetic, in your browser.
tools.method: A named individual audit recorded the following implemented fixes: Corrected ISA density-altitude inversion and physical guards; improved safe results, live controls, responsive accessible UI. The fixed status has not yet been independently rechecked.

tools.name: RAID Storage Calculator
tools.description: Work out the usable capacity, redundancy overhead and fault tolerance of a disk array for each common RAID level (0, 1, 5, 6, 10, 50, 60). Enter the number of disks and the size of each and get usable space, raw capacity, parity/mirror overhead, how many disks can fail at once, and minimum-disk validation. Useful when sizing a NAS or server array. Pure arithmetic — no rebuild-time or formatting overhead. Everything runs locally in your browser.

tools.name: Great-Circle Navigation Calculator
tools.description: Solve great-circle navigation on a spherical Earth: the initial and final compass bearing between two latitude/longitude points, the great-circle distance, the midpoint, and — in reverse — the destination reached from a start, a bearing and a distance. Two modes (point-to-point and destination) with DMS output and a compass rose. Mean Earth radius 6371 km; pure trigonometry, in your browser.

tools.name: Audio Dynamic Range & Data Rate Calculator
tools.description: Compute the theoretical dynamic range and signal-to-noise ratio of a PCM digital audio format from its bit depth (6.02·N + 1.76 dB), and the uncompressed PCM data rate and storage per minute/hour from sample rate, bit depth and channel count. Compare CD, hi-res, 24-bit studio and broadcast formats, or size storage for recording. Pure arithmetic — ideal-quantizer figures, no dither or compression. Everything runs locally in your browser.
aliases: Audio Dynamic Range and Data Rate Calculator

tools.name: NPK Fertilizer Calculator
tools.description: Work out how much nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium a fertilizer applies from its N-P-K grade and the amount spread over a lawn or garden area. Converts the oxide forms (P₂O₅, K₂O) to elemental P and K, reports pounds per 1000 ft² and per acre, and shows how much product is needed to hit a target nitrogen rate. Grade presets for common fertilizers (10-10-10, urea 46-0-0, muriate of potash 0-0-60, lawn high-N, starter). Pure arithmetic, in your browser.

tools.name: Meat Doneness & Resting Calculator
tools.description: Look up the target internal temperature for each doneness of common meats (beef, lamb, pork, poultry, fish, ground) in °F and °C, and work out the pull-from-heat temperature so that carryover cooking during the rest brings the meat up to target. Enter doneness and a carryover estimate (roast-size presets provided) and get the pull temp plus USDA food-safety guidance and rest times. Reference values for home cooks — a thermometer is the only reliable judge. Everything runs locally in your browser.

tools.name: Standard Drinks Calculator
tools.description: Convert a drink's volume and ABV into the number of standard drinks or alcohol units used in different countries — the US standard drink (14 g ethanol), the UK unit (8 g), the Australian standard drink (10 g) and an approximate EU unit. Enter volume and ABV with presets for typical beer, wine, spirits and cocktails, and get the count per region plus grams of pure ethanol, which you can carry into the BAC estimator. Pure arithmetic, in your browser.

tools.name: Field of View & Crop Factor Calculator
tools.description: Work out a camera lens's horizontal, vertical and diagonal angle of view from focal length and sensor size, plus the crop factor and the 35 mm-equivalent focal length. Sensor presets for full frame, APS-C (Sony/Nikon/Fuji and Canon), Micro 4/3, 1-inch and medium format, or a custom sensor. Useful for camera, lens and videography planning. Pure trigonometry on a rectilinear projection — fisheye projection and wide-angle edge stretch aren't modelled. Everything runs locally in your browser.
aliases: Field of View and Crop Factor Calculator

tools.name: 3D Print Filament Calculator
tools.description: Work out the mass and cost of 3D-printing filament for a print. Enter filament length (or object mass), the filament diameter and material density, and the price per kilogram or per spool; the tool gives the mass or length, the solid filament volume, the cost, and the length per kilogram. Material presets for PLA, PETG, ABS, ASA, TPU, nylon, polycarbonate, PVA, HIPS and resin. Pure arithmetic — does not account for infill, supports or print failures. Everything runs locally in your browser.

tools.name: Battery Runtime & Charge Calculator
tools.description: Estimate how long a battery will power a load and how long it takes to recharge. Enter capacity (mAh or Ah), nominal voltage and a usable-fraction derating to get watt-hours, then the load (W or A) for the runtime and the charge current and chemistry for the charge time. Useful for UPS sizing, drones, portable electronics and off-grid power. Pure arithmetic — Peukert's effect and real discharge curves aren't modelled. Everything runs locally in your browser.

tools.name: Knitting Gauge & Yarn Calculator
tools.description: Work out how many stitches to cast on and how many rows to knit from a gauge swatch and the finished project size, and estimate the yarn needed using the swatch method. Enter gauge (stitches and rows per 10 cm or per 4 inches), the project width and length, and the swatch weight and size; get cast-on count, total rows, stitch/row density, project area, and an estimated yarn weight with a safety margin. Pure arithmetic — a real blocked swatch is the only reliable basis. Everything runs locally in your browser.

tools.name: AC Sizing & Cooling Load Calculator
tools.description: Estimate the cooling capacity a room needs in BTU/h, tons and kW from its floor area, ceiling height, occupancy, kitchen and sun exposure, using the standard room-sizing rule of thumb (about 20 BTU/h per square foot, scaled for tall ceilings, extra occupants and a kitchen, with ±10% for sun). Useful for picking a window, portable or split air-conditioner; the result is rounded up to a common nominal unit size. A planning estimate only — whole-house and commercial sizing needs an ACCA Manual J calculation. Pure arithmetic, in your browser.
aliases: AC Sizing and Cooling Load Calculator
tools.method: A named individual audit recorded the following implemented fixes: Corrected load formula order/breakdown; improved validation, accessible results, and mobile UI. The fixed status has not yet been independently rechecked.

tools.name: Lighting & Illuminance Calculator
tools.description: Work out how many lumens a room needs and how many light fixtures to install from its floor area and a recommended light level. Pick a room-type preset to set the target in footcandles and lux (closet to detailed task lighting), or enter a custom value; then enter lumens per fixture and luminous efficacy to get the recommended fixture count and electrical watts. Useful for planning residential and commercial lighting and comparing LED lumen output. Pure arithmetic — the IES targets are midpoints of recommended ranges; real design also weighs fixture height, beam angle and reflectance. Everything runs locally in your browser.

tools.name: Insulation R-Value & Heat Loss Calculator
tools.description: Build up a wall, roof or floor assembly layer by layer and get its total R-value and U-factor, then estimate the conduction heat loss through a given area at a given indoor-outdoor temperature difference. Each layer's R-value is its per-inch R-value times its thickness, with inside and outside air-film resistances added on top. Useful for comparing insulation upgrades, sizing supplemental heat, and checking code R-values. Steady-state conduction only — real building heat loss also includes air infiltration, thermal bridging at studs, and solar or internal gains. Pure arithmetic, in your browser.
aliases: Insulation R-Value and Heat Loss Calculator

tools.name: Plant Spacing Calculator
tools.description: Work out how many plants fit a vegetable or flower bed for a given spacing, in square-grid or staggered (triangular, hexagonal) layout, or reverse the math to find the spacing needed to fit a target number of plants. Enter bed length and width, plant spacing and layout; get the plant count, rows and plants per row, area per plant and planting density. Staggered rows pack about 15% more plants than a square grid at the same spacing. Pure arithmetic — actual yields depend on soil, light and variety; rows are centered, so edge-planted beds may hold a few more. Everything runs locally in your browser.

tools.name: Feeds & Speeds Calculator (Milling)
tools.description: Estimate spindle RPM, feed rate and material removal rate for an end mill from the cutter diameter, number of flutes, the workpiece material's cutting speed and a per-tooth chip load. Pick a material preset to load a recommended surface speed and chip load (conservative HSS starting points) in inch (SFM) or metric (m/min) units, then adjust to suit your setup, coating and rigidity. RPM comes from surface speed divided by circumference; feed from RPM × chip load × flutes; MRR from width × depth × feed. Pure arithmetic — starting points, not a substitute for toolmaker data. Everything runs locally in your browser.

tools.name: Stopping Distance Calculator
tools.description: Estimate total stopping distance for a vehicle from its speed, the driver's reaction time and the road's grip, split into thinking distance (covered before you react) and braking distance (covered while slowing). Pick a road-condition preset to set the tyre–road friction coefficient (dry, wet, snow, ice) and a reaction-time preset, then adjust; an optional road grade lengthens or shortens the stop. Braking distance uses the constant-deceleration model v² ÷ (2·a). Useful for driver education and seeing how speed and conditions multiply stopping distance. Pure arithmetic — a real emergency stop also depends on brakes, tyres, ABS, surface and attention. Everything runs locally in your browser.

tools.name: Mechanical Advantage Calculator
tools.description: Compute the ideal mechanical advantage of the basic simple machines — a lever, a pulley system, an inclined plane, a hydraulic press and a screw — and see how the input force is amplified to move a load. Pick a machine, enter its geometry (arms, rope segments, ramp, piston radii or thread pitch) and a load, and get the mechanical advantage plus the ideal and friction-adjusted effort. Useful for physics homework, shop rigging and estimating before you build. Ideal values ignore friction, which is large for screws and real pulleys; the actual advantage is lower. Pure arithmetic, in your browser.

tools.name: True Wind Calculator
tools.description: Resolve the wind triangle for a sailing boat. Convert apparent wind (what the boat's instruments feel) into true wind over the water, or predict the apparent wind from a true-wind forecast and your course. Enter boat speed, the known wind speed and its angle off the bow (0° = headwind, 180° = dead downwind), and get the other pair with a point-of-sail label. Upwind the boat's motion inflates the apparent wind and pulls it toward the bow; downwind the boat runs away from the wind, so the apparent is lighter and further aft than true. Pure arithmetic — a velocity-triangle solution with no leeway, current, gusts or instrument calibration. Everything runs locally in your browser.

tools.name: Fabric & Sewing Yardage Calculator
tools.description: Estimate how much fabric a sewing project needs. Enter the finished piece dimensions and quantity, the fabric's width (selvedge to selvedge), the seam allowance and an optional pattern repeat, and the tool lays the cut pieces out across the bolt to give the length needed in inches/centimetres and yards/metres. Seam allowance is added to each side of every piece; the layout packs as many pieces as fit across the fabric width, then stacks the rows along the length, and flags when a piece is wider than the fabric (needing pieced panels). Useful for placemats, napkins, curtains, cushion covers and quilt blocks. Pure arithmetic — a grid layout that ignores directional prints, nap and bias; for those, add margin and round up. Everything runs locally in your browser.

tools.name: 555 Timer Calculator
tools.description: Design or analyze the classic NE555 timer in astable (free-running oscillator) or monostable (one-shot) mode. Enter the timing resistors and capacitor to get frequency, period, high and low times and duty cycle, or flip to design mode and enter a target frequency or pulse width to solve for the capacitor. The standard formulas use the internal resistor-divider thresholds at one-third and two-thirds of VCC. Useful for blinking LEDs, clock generation, debounce and time-delay circuits. Pure arithmetic — real accuracy depends on chip variant, supply voltage, capacitor tolerance and temperature, so use 1% resistors and a low-leakage cap for precision. Everything runs locally in your browser.

tools.name: Compost C:N Ratio Calculator
tools.description: Blend a pile of greens and browns and find the overall carbon-to-nitrogen ratio, the key to hot, odor-free composting. Add each ingredient with its weight and the tool sums the carbon and nitrogen by mass (from each material's C:N ratio) to give the pile's blended ratio, classifies it as too green, balanced or too brown, and suggests how much of an adjuster to add to reach the ideal ~30:1. Microbes thrive around 30:1 — too much nitrogen makes a smelly slimy pile, too much carbon stalls decomposition. Pure arithmetic — real composting also depends on moisture, aeration, particle size and temperature, so the ratio is a starting guide. Everything runs locally in your browser.

tools.name: Drip Irrigation Calculator
tools.description: Size a drip-irrigation run for a garden bed. Work out the water a runtime delivers, or the runtime needed to meet a weekly water budget. Enter the number of emitters and each emitter's flow rate, the bed area, and either a runtime or a target watering depth to get total volume, the depth applied over the bed, and a weekly schedule. Useful for vegetable beds, drip lines and container gardens — drip's low flow means runs are long but water reaches the root zone with little loss. Pure arithmetic — actual demand depends on climate, crop, soil, mulch and growth stage, so treat the depth target as a starting point. Everything runs locally in your browser.

tools.name: Retirement Withdrawal Calculator
tools.description: See how long a portfolio lasts under annual withdrawals, or find the safe withdrawal rate for a target horizon. Enter the starting balance, the yearly withdrawal, and an expected real annual return (net of inflation), and the tool steps the balance forward year by year — growing by the return, then subtracting the withdrawal — until it runs out. Flip to safe-withdrawal mode to solve for the largest yearly amount that lasts a chosen number of years. The classic 4% rule and the perpetual (never-deplete) rate are shown for context. Pure arithmetic — markets aren't smooth, returns aren't constant, withdrawals shift with spending and taxes, and sequence-of-returns risk can empty a portfolio years early, so treat the result as a planning baseline. Everything runs locally in your browser.

tools.name: Op-Amp Gain Calculator
tools.description: Analyze the three classic op-amp feedback circuits — inverting, non-inverting, and difference (differential) amplifiers. Enter the feedback and input resistors to get the closed-loop voltage gain as a ratio and in dB, and optionally add the input voltage(s) to get the output voltage, plus a gain-bandwidth product to find the small-signal bandwidth. Inverting gain is −Rf/Rin, non-inverting is 1 + Rf/Rg, and the difference amplifier subtracts its two inputs. Useful for sensor signal conditioning, audio preamps, instrumentation and active-filter stages. Pure arithmetic — ideal equations assuming infinite open-loop gain; real op-amps add bias current, offset, slew-rate and rail limits, so check the datasheet. Everything runs locally in your browser.

tools.name: Beam Deflection Calculator
tools.description: Work out the maximum deflection of a straight beam under a point load or a uniformly distributed load, for a cantilever or a simply-supported (pin-roller) span. Pick the support, the load, the material (for Young's modulus) and the cross-section, and the tool gives the area moment of inertia, the maximum deflection, and the deflection-to-span ratio compared with the common L/360 live-load and L/240 total-load limits. Standard Euler-Bernoulli formulas: cantilever end point load PL³/3EI, cantilever UDL WL³/8EI, simply-supported centre point load PL³/48EI, and simply-supported UDL 5WL³/384EI. Useful for sizing floor joists, shelves, brackets and machine frames. Pure arithmetic — small-deflection theory assuming linear-elastic material and a prismatic section; ignores shear and self-weight. Everything runs locally in your browser.

tools.name: Sun Position & Shadow Calculator
tools.description: Find the sun's elevation and azimuth at a place and time, the sunrise and sunset, the day length, and the shadow a pole casts. Enter latitude, longitude and the timezone offset of the clock time, a date and a clock time; the tool applies the equation of time and longitude correction to convert clock time to local solar time, works out the solar declination for the day, and returns the elevation and compass azimuth of the sun plus the cardinal direction. Add a pole height to see the shadow length and the direction it points. Useful for siting solar panels, photography, gardening, architecture and archaeology. Pure arithmetic — a NOAA-style simplified algorithm good to about ±0.5°; atmospheric refraction and leap years shift values slightly. Everything runs locally in your browser.

tools.name: Pump Hydraulic Power Calculator
tools.description: Size the power a pump needs from its flow rate, head and efficiency. Enter the flow, the total head, an optional pipe diameter for the flow velocity, the fluid's specific gravity, and the pump efficiency, and the tool returns the hydraulic (water) power delivered to the fluid and the brake (shaft) power the motor must supply. The core relation is power = ρ·g·Q·H divided by efficiency for input shaft power (imperial uses the equivalent HP = Q·H·SG ÷ 3960). Useful for selecting pump motors, sizing drives and checking line velocity. Pure arithmetic — a steady-state ideal-fluid relation; real systems add friction, viscosity, NPSH and cavitation limits, so size the motor with margin and consult the pump curve. Everything runs locally in your browser.

tools.name: Candy & Sugar Stages Calculator
tools.description: Identify the candy stage of boiling sugar from a thermometer reading, or find the target temperature for a stage you want — both adjusted for altitude. Sugar syrup passes through seven named stages as its temperature climbs: thread, soft ball, firm ball, hard ball, soft crack, hard crack, and caramel. Because water's boiling point falls with altitude, the whole scale shifts down by the same amount, so a high-altitude batch reaches hard crack at a lower temperature than a sea-level one. Enter your reading to name the stage, or pick a stage to get its altitude-corrected target range. Useful for fudge, caramels, nougat, toffee, brittle, lollipops and spun sugar. Pure arithmetic — the stage boundaries are long-standing culinary conventions and the altitude rule is the usual 1 °F per 500 ft (1 °C per 285 m); trust a candy thermometer and the cold-water test. Everything runs locally in your browser.

tools.name: Transformer Turns Ratio Calculator
tools.description: Solve the ideal-transformer ratios between primary and secondary voltage, current, turns and impedance. In a perfect transformer the turns ratio a = Np/Ns equals Vp/Vs and Is/Ip, and the impedance seen at the primary is a² times the load: Vp·Ip = Vs·Is and Zp = a²·Zs. Enter the primary and secondary voltage to get the turns ratio and current ratio, and optionally the load current or load impedance for the primary current, reflected impedance and apparent power. Or switch to impedance-matching mode and enter a source and load impedance to find the matching turns ratio. Useful for power-supply and mains transformer design, audio output and interstage transformers, and RF/antenna matching. Pure arithmetic — ideal lossless equations; real transformers add winding resistance, leakage inductance, core loss and frequency-dependent coupling. Everything runs locally in your browser.

tools.name: Tap Drill Calculator
tools.description: Pick the drill bit for cutting an internal thread with a tap. For a metric thread the tap drill is the major diameter minus the pitch (about 75% thread engagement); for a unified inch thread it's the major diameter minus one over the threads-per-inch. The tool computes the theoretical drill and matches it to the nearest standard bit — a fractional, number or letter drill for imperial sizes, a 0.1 mm-step metric drill for metric sizes. Useful for tapped holes in metal, 3D-printed and machined parts, and repair work. Pure arithmetic — the 75% rule balances full thread strength against a tap that doesn't bind or break; harder materials use a larger hole, softer a smaller one, and form (roll) taps need a larger pre-drill. Everything runs locally in your browser.

tools.name: Room Ventilation & CO2 Calculator
tools.description: Work out the air changes per hour (ACH) a room gets from its fresh-air supply and the steady-state CO2 level from its occupants. Enter the room dimensions and outdoor-air flow to get the volume, ACH and the time per air change; then add the number of occupants and their activity to estimate the CO2 concentration the room settles at — the balance between what people exhale and what ventilation removes — with a verdict against the 1000 ppm comfort line and the time to clear after people leave. Useful for sizing fans and exhausts for offices, classrooms, workshops and home rooms, and for checking whether a space is under-ventilated. Pure arithmetic — a single-zone well-mixed model with fixed CO2 generation rates; real rooms have imperfect mixing, varying flow and activity swings. Everything runs locally in your browser.

tools.name: Regex Explainer
tools.description: Paste a JavaScript regular expression and get a plain-English, token-by-token breakdown of what it matches — escapes, anchors, quantifiers, groups, lookarounds, character classes, backreferences and flags all named. Validates the pattern as you type, indents to show grouping, and ships a few example patterns to learn from. Pairs with the Regex Tester for trying the same pattern against real text. Everything runs locally in your browser.

tools.name: Device & Browser Info
tools.description: Inspect what your browser knows about your device — screen, viewport, browser, OS, CPU cores, memory, battery, network connection, storage quota, and ~25 feature-support checks (WebGL, WebRTC, WebAuthn, WebAssembly, Service Workers, Bluetooth, USB…). Read locally from browser APIs; nothing is uploaded.

tools.name: Profit Margin & Markup Calculator
tools.description: Convert between cost, selling price, profit, margin and markup. Pick any two known values and the rest are solved — margin is profit ÷ price, markup is profit ÷ cost (a 50% margin equals a 100% markup). Reverse-solve the price from a target margin or markup, or the cost from a price and margin. Pairs with the Break-Even, Unit Price, and Discount calculators. Everything runs locally in your browser.

tools.name: Number Sequence Generator
tools.description: Generate common number sequences — Fibonacci, Lucas, triangular, square, cube, pentagonal, hexagonal, tetrahedral, primes, powers of two, Catalan, factorial, lazy caterer, arithmetic and geometric progressions, and the Collatz hailstone. Set the term count, copy the list, and see the formula. Big-integer arithmetic keeps values exact however large they grow. Pairs with Pascal's Triangle, Prime Explorer, and Combinatorics. Runs locally in your browser.

tools.name: Open Graph & Social Meta Tag Generator
tools.description: Generate Open Graph, Twitter Card, and standard meta tags for a page — title, description, image, URL, site name, type, Twitter card style, and article author/published tags. Live social-card preview, copy-ready HTML, JSON-LD output, and a downloadable HTML stub. Pairs with the robots.txt and sitemap generators. Everything runs locally in your browser.
aliases: Open Graph and Social Meta Tag Generator

tools.name: Color Shade Scale Generator
tools.description: Generate a full 50–950 shade scale from a single base color — the way Tailwind, Radix, and Material build their color systems. Lightness stops interpolate in OKLab (a perceptual space) so the steps look even, with chroma reduction on the lightest stops so pastels don't look neon. Pick a base color and curve, then copy CSS variables, SCSS, Tailwind config, or JSON. Pairs with the Color Converter and Palette Generator. Everything runs locally in your browser.

tools.name: Image Dithering & Color Quantization
tools.description: Reduce an image to a limited palette and apply dithering — Floyd–Steinberg, Atkinson, ordered (Bayer 4×4 / 8×8), or none — with classic palettes (1-bit, Game Boy, CGA, EGA, PICO-8, Apple II, ZX Spectrum, web-safe) or your own custom colors. Downscale for chunky retro pixels. Great for pixel-art, e-ink, print, and retro-graphics workflows. Pairs with ASCII Art and Image Duotone. Everything runs locally on a canvas; nothing is uploaded.

tools.name: CSS Animation Generator
tools.description: Build CSS @keyframes animations with a live preview — pick a preset (bounce, pulse, shake, fade, slide, rotate, flip, heartbeat, rubber-band, swing, wobble, tada) or compose your own from translate, rotate, scale, skew, opacity, and blur at each keyframe stop. Set duration, delay, easing, iteration count, direction, fill mode, and play state. Copy the ready-to-paste @keyframes rule and animation shorthand. Pairs with the Cubic-Bezier Easing editor and the CSS Loader Generator. Everything runs locally in your browser.

tools.name: Media Query Generator
tools.description: Generate responsive CSS @media queries from breakpoint presets (Tailwind, Bootstrap, MUI, Foundation) or custom widths. Mix min/max width and height, orientation, prefers-color-scheme, prefers-reduced-motion, pointer, hover, and print. Combine multiple queries into a single stylesheet. Copy-ready CSS. Pairs with the CSS Grid, Type Scale, and CSS Unit Converter. Everything runs locally in your browser.

tools.name: SVG Path Visualizer
tools.description: Paste an SVG path d attribute and see it rendered with a breakdown of every command — M, L, H, V, C, S, Q, T, A, Z — plus the bounding box, total length, and command count. Toggle control-point handles, start/end markers, bounding box, grid, and stroke color. Normalize relative commands to absolute. Great for learning, debugging, and reverse-engineering path data. Pairs with the SVG Editor and SVG Optimizer. Everything runs locally in your browser.

tools.name: Text Shuffler & Scrambler
tools.description: Shuffle or scramble text six ways — shuffle words within each line, shuffle lines, shuffle all characters, shuffle characters within each word, scramble each word into a typoglycemic anagram (keep first and last letter, jumble the middle), and apply random case. Optional numeric or text seed for reproducible output. Pairs with the Text Reverser and Case Converter. Runs locally in your browser.

tools.name: Fancy Unicode Text Styler
tools.description: Convert plain text into 15 Unicode font variants — bold, italic, bold-italic, script, bold-script, fraktur, double-struck, monospace, sans-serif, sans-bold, sans-italic, circled, squared, fullwidth, and small-caps. The output is real Unicode text you can paste anywhere — social media, chat, documents. Unsupported characters pass through unchanged. Pairs with the Case Converter. Everything runs locally in your browser.

tools.name: Image Filter & Convolution Kernel
tools.description: Apply adjustable image filters — brightness, contrast, saturation, hue rotate, blur, grayscale, sepia, invert — and run a custom 3×3 convolution kernel (sharpen, edge detect, emboss, box blur, Gaussian, Sobel X/Y, Laplacian, or your own matrix with divisor and offset). Filter presets (vivid, warm, cool, vintage, noir, invert) and side-by-side preview. Download as PNG. Pairs with Image Duotone, Image Dithering, and Image Histogram. Everything runs locally on a canvas; nothing is uploaded.

tools.name: CSS Flexbox Generator
tools.description: Build a CSS flexbox layout visually and copy the generated CSS. Set the container's flex-direction, flex-wrap, justify-content, align-items, align-content, gap, and padding; control each item's flex-grow, flex-shrink, flex-basis, align-self, and order. Live preview, add/remove items. Pairs with the CSS Grid Generator. Everything runs locally in your browser.

tools.name: Circle of Fifths

tools.name: Round Robin Scheduler
tools.description: Build a round-robin fixture list for 2 to 24 teams: every pair meets once or home and away, byes are handled, home advantage stays balanced, and the schedule can be copied or downloaded.
tools.method: Circle-method round robin construction. Teams occupy fixed slots; each round pairs slot i with slot n-1-i, then all slots except the first rotate one place. For an odd team count a bye placeholder is added, so every team sits out exactly one round and plays every other team once. A second leg repeats the schedule with home and away reversed. Home advantage is assigned greedily to the team with fewer home games, then improved by flipping individual fixtures whenever one moves a home game from a team with at least two more home games to one with fewer; the result gives every team the same number of home games in a double round robin and a spread of at most one in a single one. Fixtures inside a round are listed by lowest team position. Teams are unseeded: there is no strength balancing, travel or venue optimisation, and no dates are assigned.

tools.name: Fishing Line Capacity Calculator
tools.description: Estimate how much line a reel spool holds from its arbor, lip and width, and work out how much braid backing to wind before a set mono topshot finishes at the fill line.
tools.method: Line is modelled as concentric layers wound on the spool. Each layer adds one line diameter to the wound radius and holds spool width divided by line diameter turns at its mean diameter, discounted by the winding density for loose, criss-crossed laying (85% by default). The capacity is the sum of those layer lengths from the arbor to the fill line, which is the lip diameter less twice the fill gap because the gap is radial. A line thicker than the radial fill depth cannot be wound. For the two-line plan the braid goes on first and the topshot last: the interface diameter where a band of the requested topshot length ends exactly at the fill line is found by bisection, and the braid backing is the fill of the band from the arbor to that diameter. If the topshot does not fit even on the bare spool, the plan reports the largest topshot the spool holds instead of inventing a backing length. Measurements come from the reel itself, and published capacities assume a fuller spool, so results are planning estimates rather than a replacement for the maker's rating.

Every five-card combination of the picked cards (one for five cards, six for six, twenty-one for seven) is scored and the strongest kept, so a seven-card hand reports the best five. A hand is classified as straight flush, four of a kind, full house, flush, straight, three of a kind, two pair, one pair or high card; straights need five consecutive ranks with the ace allowed low as A-2-3-4-5, and a flush needs all five cards in one suit. Ties inside a category are broken by the ranks that make the hand and then by kickers in descending order, which is the usual poker order: pair rank then three kickers; higher pair, lower pair, then kicker; triplet then two kickers; quad then kicker; triplet then pair; and for flushes and high cards all five ranks in order. Suits never rank. Assumes a standard deck with no duplicate cards. Wild cards, jokers, short-deck and lowball variants are not supported, and the tool gives no odds, equity or betting advice.

tools.name: Interval Ear Trainer
tools.description: Train your ear to recognise musical intervals: the trainer plays two notes and you name the distance between them, low to high, high to low or together, with a running accuracy and streak. Runs locally in your browser.
tools.method: The trainer draws an interval from a fixed level pool and plays two synthesised notes from a random root in 12-tone equal temperament, with A4 = 440 Hz and frequency = 440 x 2^((MIDI - 69)/12). Beginner offers the major third, perfect fourth, perfect fifth and perfect octave; intermediate adds the major second, minor third and major sixth; advanced offers every interval from the minor second to the perfect octave. Ascending and harmonic questions pick a root from MIDI 55-71 (G3-B4) and descending questions from MIDI 60-76 (C4-E5), so both notes stay within a comfortable listening range. A question never repeats the previous interval while the pool holds more than one choice. Answers are checked by semitone count; the score tracks questions asked, correct answers, current streak and best streak, and accuracy is correct divided by asked, rounded to a whole percent. Notes are generated locally with the Web Audio API and a short triangle-wave envelope: no audio files, no microphone input and no network requests. This is interval recognition practice only, not absolute-pitch, tuning or intonation training.

tools.name: Skyscraper Puzzle
tools.description: Fill an N×N grid with towers of heights 1 to N so every row and column contains each height once, using the visibility clues around the edge: a taller tower hides every shorter one behind it. Includes 4×4, 5×5 and 6×6 puzzles at three difficulties, with mistake checking, a timer and keyboard controls.
tools.method: A puzzle starts from a Latin square: the cyclic square has its rows, columns and symbols shuffled, and the four visibility counts (seen from the top, bottom, left and right of every line) are computed. Clues are then removed one at a time in random order; a removal is kept only when an exhaustive search still finds exactly one solution, and puzzles that cannot reach the difficulty target are discarded and rebuilt. The search enforces each row and column as an all-different set, chooses the empty cell with the fewest legal heights, and prunes a line when its visible-tower count can no longer reach the clue: the count of records in the filled prefix is a lower bound and that count plus the unfilled positions is an upper bound. Difficulty is the number of clues left: 4×4 keeps 12, 9 or 7 of 16; 5×5 keeps 16, 12 or 9 of 20; 6×6 keeps 20, 15 or 11-13 of 24. A 6×6 build takes about a second in a browser, so the page serves 6×6 puzzles from a fixed set of 24 that were generated and uniqueness-checked the same way, eight per difficulty. Answers are checked against the single stored solution, and repeated heights in a row or column are flagged as you type. Everything runs in this page: no network requests, accounts, uploads or stored data.

tools.name: Bingo Card Generator
tools.description: Turn your own word or phrase list into printable bingo cards. Pick 3×3, 4×4 or 5×5 grids, generate up to 30 cards with different layouts, add a free centre space, and copy a shuffled call list.

tools.name: Audio Sync Drift Calculator
tools.description: Estimate how far separately recorded sound drifts against picture from a clock mismatch: drift per minute, drift at the end of a take, when to re-sync and the playback-rate correction that removes it.
tools.method: Drift after a take is the clock mismatch in parts per million multiplied by the take length: 1,000 ppm (0.1%) over 1,200 seconds is 1.2 seconds. Drift per minute is 60 x ppm / 1,000,000, and the same drift counted in frames uses the chosen timeline rate. Spacing between re-sync marks is the allowed drift in frames divided by (frame rate x mismatch), and the number of marks is the take length divided by that spacing, rounded up; when the drift at the end already fits the allowance, no mid-take marks are reported. The speed correction is 1 + ppm/1,000,000 in one direction and its reciprocal in the other. Presets cover the 48.048 kHz film-sound mismatch and the 23.976/24 and 29.97/30 timebase mismatches, all at 1,000 ppm; custom values are limited to 1-10,000 ppm. Take length is limited to 12 hours and the drift allowance to 0.1-120 frames. Whether sound ends up early or late depends on which clock runs fast, so both correction directions are shown. Everything runs locally with no file access, upload or storage.

tools.name: Uncompressed Video Data Rate Calculator
tools.description: Calculate the raw data rate, per-frame size and storage of uncompressed video from frame size, frame rate, chroma sampling and bit depth, and see which SDI interface carries it.
tools.method: Raw video is measured sample by sample: every pixel carries one luma sample and the chroma sampling adds one full colour sample per pixel for 4:4:4, one per two pixels for 4:2:2 and one per two pixels in both directions for 4:2:0, so the samples per pixel are 3, 2, 1.5 and 1 for monochrome. Bits per pixel is samples per pixel times bits per sample; the frame size in pixels times bits per pixel is the bits per frame, and multiplying by the frame rate gives the raw payload in bits per second. Dividing by eight and scaling gives bytes, with decimal storage units (1 GB = 10^9 bytes). The interface is the smallest nominal SMPTE payload rate (270 Mb/s SD-SDI, 1.485 Gb/s HD-SDI, 2.97 Gb/s 3G-SDI, 5.94 Gb/s 6G-SDI, 11.88 Gb/s 12G-SDI) that is at least the raw rate, and its utilisation is the ratio of the two. Blanking intervals, ancillary data, embedded audio and frame padding are not part of the count, so a real signal needs headroom above the bare payload figure.

tools.name: Rectangular Waveguide Calculator
tools.description: Calculate the TE10 cutoff frequency and single-mode band of an air-filled rectangular waveguide from its broad and narrow wall, with the next higher mode, guide wavelength, phase and group velocity and TE10 wave impedance at an operating frequency.
tools.method: For an air-filled rectangular guide with broad wall a and narrow wall b, the dominant TE10 mode cuts off at fc = c / 2a with c = 299,792,458 m/s; TE20 cuts off at c / a, TE01 at c / 2b and TE11/TM11 at (c/2)·sqrt(1/a² + 1/b²). The lower of the TE20 and TE01 cutoffs is reported as the next mode and marks the top of the single-mode range, while the usable band is shown as 1.25 to 1.9 times the TE10 cutoff. At an operating frequency f above cutoff, the guide wavelength is the free-space wavelength divided by sqrt(1 - (fc/f)²), phase velocity is c divided by the same factor, group velocity is c times it, and the TE10 wave impedance is the free-space impedance (376.73 Ω) divided by it, so phase and group velocity multiply to c². Below cutoff the mode is evanescent and no wavelength or impedance is reported. A homogeneous dielectric filling would scale every cutoff by 1/sqrt(εr) and is not modelled.

tools.name: Golf Course Handicap Calculator
tools.description: Turn a golf Handicap Index into a course handicap and playing handicap for the tees played, and convert a gross score into a World Handicap System score differential.
tools.method: The course handicap is Handicap Index × Slope Rating ÷ 113 + (Course Rating − Par), rounded to the nearest whole number with halves rounded away from zero; a negative result is a plus handicap. The playing handicap is the rounded course handicap multiplied by the allowance percentage and rounded the same way; 95% is the WHS default for individual stroke play. tools.name: Frame Rate Conform Calculator
tools.description: Conform a clip between frame rates and see the new running time, the speed change, the frames to duplicate or drop, and the audio pitch shift.
tools.method: A speed conform keeps every frame and plays the clip at the target rate, so the playback factor is target fps divided by source fps: 24 to 25 fps runs at 1.0417x, 4.17% faster. The frame count is duration x source fps rounded to the nearest whole frame, the conformed duration is that frame count divided by the target rate, and the same-length alternative reports how many frames a frame-for-frame conform would duplicate (target rate higher) or drop (target rate lower). Audio that is not retimed shifts by 12 x log2(target / source) semitones, with no pitch correction applied. Inputs are limited to 1-240 fps and 0.1-86,400 s; frame rates within 0.002 fps of 23.976, 24, 25, 29.97 and 30 are treated as the named rate for the PAL and 0.1% pull-up notes. Drop-frame timecode, interlaced field order, 3:2 pulldown, motion blur and any pitch-correcting retime are not modelled, whole-frame rounding matters for very short clips, and a clip that rounds to zero frames at the source rate is rejected. The calculation runs entirely in the browser with no storage, uploads or network access.

tools.name: Transposing Instrument Calculator
tools.description: Convert written pitch to concert pitch for transposing instruments, with the interval, octave shift and a chromatic reference chart.
tools.method: Concert pitch is the written pitch shifted by the instrument's transposition: a Bb trumpet sounds a major 2nd below written, an Eb alto saxophone a major 6th below, an F horn a perfect 5th below, an Eb clarinet a minor 3rd above, and the piccolo, guitar, double bass and contrabassoon move whole octaves. Each instrument is stored as a semitone and letter-step offset so the result keeps a musical spelling: a written Db on a Bb clarinet sounds Cb, while a written C# sounds B. The interval name follows from the letter distance and semitone count, so compound shifts are named as major 9ths and major 13ths, and the concert frequency is 440 x 2^((MIDI - 69) / 12) in 12-tone equal temperament. Notes use scientific pitch notation (C4 is middle C), octaves are limited to -1 to 9 and pitches to MIDI 0-127, and the chart lists every chromatic step of the entered octave. Key signatures, clefs, written accidentals carried through a key change, horn basso and other historical notations, bass-clef readings for bass clarinet, euphonium and tuba, and instrument ranges or playability are not modelled; the calculation runs entirely in the browser with no storage, uploads or network access.

tools.name: Receiver Sensitivity Calculator
tools.description: Calculate receiver sensitivity in dBm from noise figure, bandwidth, required SNR and temperature, with the noise floor and equivalent 50 ohm voltage.
tools.method: Receiver sensitivity is the thermal noise power in the receiver bandwidth plus the receiver noise figure plus the signal-to-noise ratio the demodulator needs: Pmin = 10 log10(k T B) + NF + SNR, reported in dBm with k = 1.380649e-23 J/K, T in kelvin, B in hertz and NF and SNR in dB. At the reference temperature of 290 K the thermal noise density is about -173.98 dBm/Hz, which is the familiar -174 dBm/Hz figure. The noise floor in the chosen bandwidth is reported separately, together with the equivalent RMS voltage across a matched 50 ohm load from V = sqrt(P R) and the signal power in watts. The reference table recomputes the noise floor and sensitivity for 3 kHz, 12.5 kHz, 25 kHz, 200 kHz, 1 MHz and 20 MHz using the entered noise figure, SNR and temperature. Bandwidth accepts hertz, kilohertz or megahertz and is limited to 1 THz, noise figure to 0-100 dB, required SNR to -100 to 100 dB (negative values model spreading and coding gain) and temperature to 1-10,000 K. The estimate assumes a flat noise figure across the band, a receiver noise figure that already includes feedline loss ahead of the receiver, and a matched 50 ohm system for the voltage; it does not model interference, phase noise, spurs, fading, coding gain, antenna noise or a complete link budget, and it runs entirely in the browser with no storage, uploads or network access.

sources.title: H. T. Friis, Noise Figures of Radio Receivers, Proceedings of the IRE, 1944 (noise figure definition)
ITU-R P.372, Radio Noise (reference noise temperature and noise density)
D. M. Pozar, Microwave Engineering, 4th ed. (thermal noise, noise figure and receiver sensitivity)

tools.name: Fish Weight Calculator
tools.description: Estimate a fish's weight in pounds, kilograms and ounces from its length and girth, with a table showing how the shape factor changes the answer.
aliases: Fish Weight From Length and Girth
fish weight from length and girth
tools.method: Weight is estimated with the standard length-girth field formula W = L * G^2 / K, where L is the length from snout to tail fork with the tail pinched, G is the girth around the widest part of the body with the fins folded, both measured in inches, and K is a shape factor of 800 by default; the result is reported in pounds, kilograms at 0.45359237 kg per pound, and ounces at 16 per pound. The same fish is recomputed at shape factors of 700, 800, 900 and 1000 to show how much body shape moves the estimate, and the girth-to-length ratio is reported as a condition indicator. Length accepts 1-100 in (2.5-254 cm) and girth 0.5-100 in (1.3-254 cm), with centimetre input converted exactly at 2.54 cm per inch; girth may not exceed the length, and the shape factor is limited to 400-2000. Species, condition factor, spawn state, stomach contents, girth measurement error and the divergence of very large or very slender fish from the formula are not modelled, so the result is an estimate that can be off by roughly a tenth either way and is no substitute for a scale. The calculation runs entirely in the browser with no storage, uploads or network access.

tools.name: Shutter Angle Calculator
tools.description: Convert a shutter angle to a shutter speed at any frame rate, or the reverse, with the exposure time, frame interval and the exposure change against a 180° shutter.
tools.method: A shutter angle is the fraction of each frame for which the shutter is open, so the exposure time is the angle divided by 360 and by the frame rate: 180 degrees at 24 fps is 0.5 / 24 = 1/48 s, and 172.8 degrees at 24 fps is exactly 1/50 s, the usual setting for shooting under 50 Hz lighting. The calculator also solves the inverse, angle = 360 x shutter speed x frame rate, accepting a shutter speed in seconds or as a fraction such as 1/48. It reports the shutter speed as a fraction and in milliseconds, the frame interval, the percentage of each frame the shutter is open, and the exposure change in stops relative to a 180 degree shutter, plus a table of 45, 90, 144, 172.8, 180, 270 and 360 degrees at the entered rate. Frame rates are limited to 1-240 fps, angles to 1-360 degrees, and a shutter speed may not be longer than one frame interval. The conversion assumes the whole frame is exposed at once; rolling-shutter readout, lighting flicker, aperture and ND filtration are not modelled. The calculation runs entirely in the browser with no storage, uploads or network access.

tools.name: Quilt Backing Calculator
tools.description: Size quilt backing from the quilt top: the cut size with margin, lengthwise panels or crosswise strips, the seam allowance, yardage to buy and the batting size.
tools.method: Backing is cut larger than the quilt top and is often pieced from standard-width fabric. The calculator adds the entered margin to all four sides of the top, so a 60 x 72 in top with a 4 in margin needs a 68 x 80 in cut. It then costs both layouts: n lengthwise panels, each usable-width wide and the full cut length long, joined along their long edges, and m crosswise strips, each the full cut width long and usable-width tall, joined across. With a seam allowance s, n pieces of usable width w cover n*w - (n-1)*s, so n is the smallest count that reaches the needed span; each layout's yardage is its piece count times the length cut from the bolt divided by 36. The layout with the smaller yardage is recommended, ties going to lengthwise panels, and the buy amount is rounded up to the next 1/8 yard. Batting is reported at the same cut size as the backing. Directional prints that cannot be rotated, long-arm frame requirements, and fabric shrinkage are not modelled. The calculation runs entirely in the browser with no storage, uploads or network access.

tools.name: Vocal Range Calculator
tools.description: Turn the lowest and highest notes a singer can comfortably reach into a range: the span in semitones and octaves, the frequency limits, and which standard voice ranges contain or overlap it.
tools.method: Notes are read as scientific pitch notation, with C4 at MIDI 60 and A4 at the 440 Hz reference, so a note's MIDI number is (octave + 1) x 12 plus its pitch class and accidental. Frequencies follow 12-tone equal temperament: f = 440 x 2^((midi - 69) / 12). The range is the difference between the two MIDI numbers, split into whole octaves and remaining semitones, and its frequency ratio is 2^(semitones / 12). Six common classical and choral reference ranges are compared: a range is reported as containing the singer's notes when both reference endpoints lie outside the sung range, as overlapping when the two spans share at least one pitch, and otherwise as outside, and the narrowest containing range is named. Head voice, falsetto, passaggio, tessitura and any Fach classification are not modelled, and reference ranges differ between traditions, so the comparison is descriptive rather than a diagnosis. The calculation runs entirely in the browser with no storage, uploads or network access.

tools.name: Intermodulation Product Calculator
tools.description: List the intermodulation, sum and harmonic products of two or three carrier frequencies up to a chosen order, and flag the products that land inside a protect band.
tools.method: Each product is a whole-number combination m1f1 + m2f2 (plus m3f3 when a third carrier is entered), and its order is the sum of the absolute values of the coefficients, so 2f1 - f2 is third order and 3f1 - 2f2 is fifth. Every coefficient triple from minus the chosen order to plus the chosen order is enumerated, kept when that absolute sum lies between two and the chosen order and the resulting frequency is positive, and rounded to six decimal places in MHz. Products that share a frequency are listed once, keeping the lowest order that produces them, because lower orders are normally the stronger products; the list is then sorted by frequency. Single-carrier harmonics such as 2f1 and 3f2 are included. A protect band, given as a low and a high limit, marks each product whose frequency falls on or inside those limits. Frequencies must be greater than zero and at most 1,000,000 MHz, orders run from 2 to 7, and the protect band requires both limits with the low one below the high one. The model is frequency arithmetic only: it does not consider transmit levels, mixer intercept points, receiver selectivity, antenna coupling, spectral masks or the applicable band plan, so it is not an interference or authorisation determination. Everything runs in the browser with no storage, uploads or network access.

tools.name: Track Lane Stagger Calculator
tools.description: Calculate the start-line stagger, lap length, bend radii and running-surface area for every lane of a 400 m running track from the lane width and straight length.
tools.method: A 400 m oval is two equal straights joined by two semicircles, so the lane 1 measurement radius is (400 - 2 x straight) / 2pi. Lanes 2 and outward are measured 20 cm from the line on their inside edge, while lane 1 is measured 30 cm from the kerb or, where there is no kerb, 20 cm from a painted line. The 400 m stagger for lane n is therefore 2pi x ((n - 1) x lane width + 0.20 - lane 1 offset): with 1.22 m lanes off a 30 cm kerb that gives 7.04, 14.70, 22.37, 30.03, 37.70, 45.36 and 53.03 m, and measuring lane 1 from a painted line instead gives 7.67, 15.33, 23.00, 30.66, 38.33, 45.99 and 53.66 m. Each lane's 400 m length is 400 m plus its stagger, and the 200 m stagger is half the 400 m figure because a 200 m race covers one bend. The inner edge radius is the lane 1 measurement radius minus its offset, the outer radius adds one lane width per lane, and the running-surface area is the ring between those radii plus the two straights. Inputs are 2 to 10 lanes, a lane width of 0.9 to 1.5 m and straights of 40 to 120 m. This is planning arithmetic only: it assumes a two-straight 400 m oval, and it does not survey a track, set competition markings or certify a facility. Everything runs in the browser with no storage, uploads or network access.

tools.name: GOP Length Calculator
tools.description: Convert a keyframe interval in seconds to a whole-frame GOP length at any frame rate, or the reverse, with keyframes per clip and a table of common intervals.
tools.method: A keyframe interval in seconds and a GOP length in frames describe the same encoder setting, so the GOP length is the interval multiplied by the frame rate, rounded to a whole frame: 2 s at 25 fps is 50 frames, while 2 s at 29.97 fps is 59.94 frames and becomes a 60-frame GOP with an effective interval of 2.002 s. The calculator also solves the inverse, dividing the frame count by the frame rate, and reports the exact value before rounding, the effective interval, the frames in the clip, the number of GOPs that start in it (one per interval plus the opening frame, rounded up), keyframes per minute, and a table of 0.5, 1, 2, 4 and 10 s intervals at the entered rate. Frame rates are limited to 1-240 fps, intervals to 0.1-60 s, GOP lengths to 1-20,000 frames and clip durations to 1-86,400 s, and a GOP is never shorter than one frame. The result is planning arithmetic; encoders may cap the GOP or insert extra keyframes at scene cuts, which are not modelled. The calculation runs entirely in the browser with no storage, uploads or network access.

tools.name: Weaving Warp Calculator
tools.description: Plan a weaving warp: finished length and a take-up allowance give warp length per item and in total, sett and width give the ends, and the totals convert to warp yarn in yards and metres.
tools.method: Warp length per item is the finished length plus the take-up and shrinkage allowance: finished length x (1 + allowance / 100). The total warp is the item warp multiplied by the number of items, plus the loom waste and fringe once at the start of the warp. Ends in the warp are the sett in ends per inch multiplied by the width in the reed, rounded to a whole end (half up). Warp yarn is ends x total warp length, converted from inches to yards (divide by 36) and to metres (x 0.0254). The reed table lists reeds of 6, 8, 10, 12, 15, 20 and 25 dents per inch with the closest whole number of ends per dent from 1 to 4, since sleying more than one end per dent is how weavers reach a sett a single dent pattern cannot give. Lengths are limited to 1-200 in per item, 0-120 in of waste, 1-200 items, a 0-50% allowance, a sett of 1-60 ends per inch and a reed width of 1-120 in. The allowance is one planning figure because take-up and shrinkage depend on weave structure, yarn and finishing; fringe and sampling are not modelled. The calculation runs entirely in the browser with no storage, uploads or network access.

sources.title: Handweaving warp planning: warp length = finished length x (1 + take-up allowance) + loom waste, with the waste and fringe counted once for the whole warp
Sett (ends per inch) x width in the reed = number of warp ends; common reeds are sleyed with 1-4 ends per dent to reach a target sett

tools.name: String Tension Calculator
tools.description: Calculate a musical string's tension from its unit weight, scale length and pitch in pounds, kilograms and newtons, with a plain-steel gauge table for the selected note.
tools.method: Frequency comes from the note in scientific pitch notation with A4 fixed at 440 Hz: f = 440 x 2^((MIDI - 69) / 12), where MIDI = (octave + 1) x 12 + semitones above C, so E4 is 329.63 Hz. Tension is T = 4 x mu x L^2 x f^2 newtons, with mu the unit weight converted from grams per metre to kilograms per metre and L the scale length converted from inches to metres. Newtons convert to pounds by dividing by 4.4482216152605 and to kilograms by dividing by 9.80665. The equivalent plain-steel gauge inverts the same relation for a solid string at 7.85 g/cm3, d = sqrt(4 x mu / (pi x rho)), and the gauge table applies it to plain-steel diameters from 0.008 to 0.026 in at the selected pitch and scale length. Wound strings carry wrap as well as a core, so their published unit weight should be used rather than a solid-cylinder estimate. Inputs are limited to a scale length of 8-40 in and a unit weight of 0.02-30 g/m. The calculation runs entirely in the browser with no storage, uploads or network access.

sources.title: Mersenne's law: a stretched string's tension is T = 4 mu L^2 f^2, where mu is mass per unit length, L the vibrating length and f the frequency
Equal temperament with A4 = 440 Hz: each semitone multiplies frequency by 2^(1/12), and a plain steel string has mu = (pi/4) d^2 rho at about 7.85 g/cm3

tools.name: Erlang B Trunking Calculator
tools.description: Calculate Erlang B blocking probability and carried traffic for a group of telephone trunks from offered traffic in erlangs, and find the trunk count a grade of service needs.
tools.method: Offered traffic A in erlangs is the busy-hour load: call attempts per hour multiplied by average holding time in seconds, divided by 3600. Erlang B models a group of n trunks with Poisson arrivals, blocked calls cleared and no retries: B(0) = 1 and B(n) = A x B(n-1) / (n + A x B(n-1)), evaluated iteratively in double precision up to 1,500 trunks, so the blocking probability for the entered trunk count is B at that index. Carried traffic is A x (1 - B) erlangs and blocked traffic is A x B. The trunk count a grade of service needs is the smallest n whose B x 100 is at or below the target blocking percentage, searched from 1 upwards; the table lists the seven trunk counts around that minimum with their blocking and carried load. Inputs are limited to 0.01-1,000 erlangs, 1-1,500 trunks and a 0.01-50% target. The calculation is a planning estimate that assumes one overflow-free group and runs entirely in the browser with no storage, uploads or network access.

sources.title: Erlang B blocking formula: B(0) = 1 and B(n) = A x B(n-1) / (n + A x B(n-1)), the fraction of calls refused when blocked calls are cleared
Erlang as a unit of traffic intensity: one erlang is one circuit occupied for the whole hour, so busy-hour call attempts x mean holding time / 3600 gives the load

tools.name: Contact Sheet Planner
tools.description: Plan a video contact sheet: evenly spaced sample timestamps and frame numbers, thumbnail size from the source aspect ratio, and the exact pixel size of the finished grid.
tools.method: Each thumbnail samples the centre of an equal slice of the clip, so the sampling interval is duration divided by the number of thumbnails and sample i sits at (i + 0.5) times that interval. A sample's frame number is its timestamp times the frame rate, rounded to the nearest whole frame and clamped to the clip's last frame, where the clip holds the frame rate times duration rounded to whole frames. Thumbnail height is the thumbnail width times the source height divided by the source width, rounded to a whole pixel, which keeps the source aspect ratio without letterboxing. A tile is the thumbnail plus its caption band, rows are the thumbnail count divided by the columns rounded up, and the sheet is twice the margin plus the columns' width plus the gaps across, and twice the margin plus the rows' tiles plus the gaps down. Empty cells fill the last row. The page assumes a constant frame rate, does not decode, render or upload any video, and does not model drop-frame timecode or per-platform sprite-sheet limits.

tools.name: Song Form Duration Calculator
tools.description: Calculate a song arrangement's duration from tempo, time signature, section bars and repeats, with a start-to-finish timeline for every section.
tools.method: A tempo beat lasts 60/BPM seconds. A bar contains meterBeats × 4 ÷ (meterUnit × tempo beat's quarter-note length) tempo beats, where whole, half, quarter, dotted-quarter, eighth and sixteenth notes have quarter-note lengths 4, 2, 1, 1.5, 0.5 and 0.25 respectively. Each section performs bars × repeats bars; its duration is performed bars × beats per bar × 60/BPM. Section durations are summed in order to produce the timeline and total. Written bars omit repeats; performed bars include them. Pickup bars, gaps, fermatas and tempo changes are outside the model. Inputs and results remain unrounded in the calculation core; only displayed times are rounded to tenths of a second.

tools.name: Badminton Scorekeeper
tools.description: Keep a best-of-three badminton match score with rally scoring, deuce, the 30-point cap, serving side, game history, undo and change-of-ends prompts.
tools.method: BWF rally-scoring state machine: the rally winner gains one point and becomes the serving side. A game ends at 21 with a two-point lead from 20-all, or immediately at 30; the game winner serves first in the next game. Two game wins end the best-of-three match. Even serving-side scores indicate the right service court and odd scores the left. A change-of-ends event is emitted when either side first reaches 11 in game three. Undo restores the complete prior state, and scoring is refused after the match. Individual doubles player rotation, intervals, lets and umpire decisions are not modelled. Names and scores remain only in page memory.

tools.name: Video RGB to YCbCr Converter
tools.description: Convert 8-bit RGB and YCbCr values using BT.601, BT.709 or BT.2020 matrices, with full or limited range, exact values, rounded code values, round trips and clipping detection.
tools.method: For gamma-encoded 8-bit R′G′B′, luma is Y′ = Kr R′ + (1 − Kr − Kb) G′ + Kb B′ on channels normalized to 0–1. Cb = (B′ − Y′) / (2(1 − Kb)) and Cr = (R′ − Y′) / (2(1 − Kr)). BT.601 uses Kr 0.299 and Kb 0.114, BT.709 uses 0.2126 and 0.0722, and BT.2020 non-constant-luminance conversion uses 0.2627 and 0.058. Limited range emits 16 + 219Y′ and 128 + 224Cb/Cr; full range emits 255Y′ and 127.5 + 255Cb/Cr. Codes are rounded to the nearest integer and clipped to their selected 8-bit ranges. Inverse conversion algebraically reconstructs R′ and B′ from Cr and Cb, then G′ from luma, and flags any unrounded RGB channel outside 0–255 before clipping. The round trip uses the quantized output codes. This tool does not linearize RGB, change transfer characteristics or primaries, process constant-luminance Y′CbcCrc, interpret HDR metadata, or decode media.

tools.name: Erlang C Call Queue Calculator
tools.description: Calculate call-queue probability, average waiting time and service level with Erlang C, and find the simultaneous agent count a target needs.
tools.method: Offered traffic A in erlangs is busy-hour calls multiplied by average handle time in seconds, divided by 3600. For N agents, first evaluate Erlang B with B(0) = 1 and B(n) = A x B(n-1) / (n + A x B(n-1)). When N is greater than A, Erlang C queue probability is C = B(N) / (1 - (A/N) x (1 - B(N))). Average wait across all calls is C x H/(N-A), average wait once queued is H/(N-A), and service level within t seconds is 1 - C x exp(-(N-A) x t/H), where H is average handle time. At or above full occupancy (N less than or equal to A), no steady-state queue probability, wait or service level is reported. The target agent count is the smallest stable N up to 1,500 whose service level meets the entered percentage. Inputs allow up to 36,000 calls/hour and 3,600-second handle times, with offered load capped at 1,000 erlangs. This planning estimate assumes Poisson arrivals, exponential handle times, identical agents, an unlimited queue and no abandonment or retries; it reports concurrent agents before shrinkage, not roster headcount.

sources.title: Erlang C delay formula for an M/M/N queue: C = B / (1 - (A/N)(1-B)), where B is the corresponding Erlang B blocking probability and N > A

Erlang as a unit of traffic intensity: busy-hour calls x mean handle time / 3600

tools.name: Tennis Scorekeeper
tools.description: Keep a best-of-three tennis match score with advantage scoring, six-game sets, seven-point tiebreaks, set history and undo.
tools.method: Standard tennis scoring state machine: a regular game ends when a player has at least four points and a two-point lead, with 0, 15, 30, 40, deuce and advantage labels. tools.name: Knitting Shaping Calculator
tools.description: Distribute knitting increases or decreases evenly across one row or round and get an exact, copyable stitch pattern using M1, KFB, k2tog or ssk.
tools.method: The absolute difference between the current and target stitch counts is the number of shaping groups. Divide the current stitches by that group count: every group receives the integer quotient, and the remainder is distributed one extra original stitch at a time using cumulative Bresenham-style rounding, so group sizes differ by at most one and their sum always equals the current count. For M1, the listed knit or purl stitches are followed by the increase, which consumes no original stitch. KFB reserves one original stitch for the shaping operation; k2tog and ssk reserve two. The remaining group stitches are worked as knit or purl before that operation. Identical adjacent instructions are compressed into repeat counts. One-row mode permits at most one shaping action per original-stitch group: increases cannot exceed the current count, and the target of a decrease cannot be below half the current count rounded up. No-change input produces an instruction to work every stitch.

tools.name: Constellation Diagram Explorer
tools.description: Map binary sequences to BPSK, QPSK, 8-PSK, 16-QAM and 64-QAM constellation points with normalized I/Q coordinates and Gray-coded labels.
tools.method: Whitespace is removed from a sequence of at most 96 binary digits, which must form complete groups for the selected scheme. BPSK maps 0 and 1 to -1 and +1 on the I axis. QPSK uses 00, 01, 11 and 10 counter-clockwise from the positive I, positive Q quadrant, with each coordinate divided by sqrt(2). 8-PSK uses the cyclic Gray sequence 000, 001, 011, 010, 110, 111, 101 and 100 at 45-degree intervals starting on the positive I axis. Square QAM independently maps the first half of each label to I and the second half to Q using reflected Gray level sequences: 00, 01, 11, 10 select -3, -1, +1, +3 divided by sqrt(10) for 16-QAM; 000, 001, 011, 010, 110, 111, 101, 100 select -7, -5, -3, -1, +1, +3, +5, +7 divided by sqrt(42) for 64-QAM. Each full constellation therefore has unit average power. Coordinates are copied to four decimal places; calculations retain full precision. This is an educational mapping reference, not a modem configuration or link-performance calculator.

tools.name: Video Loop Planner
tools.description: Plan complete video clip repeats and the final partial pass needed to fill a target runtime, with whole-frame counts and a copyable edit plan.
tools.method: Clip duration, target runtime and frame rate are parsed as decimal values with at most three decimal places. Each duration is multiplied by the frame rate and rounded to the nearest whole frame, with values rounding below one frame rejected. Complete loops are the target frame count divided by the clip frame count and rounded down. The remainder is the final partial pass; total passes are complete loops plus one when a remainder exists. If the target is shorter than the clip, there are zero complete loops and one partial pass. If there is no remainder, the target ends exactly on a loop boundary and needs no partial pass. Displayed seconds and source out-points are derived from frame counts divided by the frame rate, so rounding remains explicit. Inputs are limited to 0.001-86,400 seconds and 1-240 fps. The tool assumes constant-frame-rate planning arithmetic and does not inspect media, model drop-frame timecode, create seamless transitions or render a video. It stores and transmits nothing.

tools.name: Digital Line Coding Visualizer
tools.description: Turn binary data into NRZ-L, NRZ-I, Manchester, differential Manchester and bipolar AMI waveforms with transition and mean-level summaries.
tools.method: Whitespace is removed from a sequence of 1-64 binary digits. NRZ-L maps 0 to low (-1) and 1 to high (+1). NRZ-I starts low, changes level at the start of a 1 and holds the previous level for a 0. Manchester follows IEEE 802.3: 0 is low-to-high and 1 is high-to-low. Differential Manchester starts low, always changes at mid-bit, adds a start-bit transition for 0 and no start-bit transition for 1. Bipolar AMI holds zero for 0 and maps successive 1 bits to alternating full-bit positive and negative pulses, starting positive. Each bit is represented by two half-bit levels; transitions count changes between adjacent levels, and the mean is their arithmetic average. The SVG waveform and copyable level list are deterministic and use only normalized -1, 0 and +1 values. No data is stored or transmitted.

tools.name: OFDM Symbol Timing Calculator
tools.description: Calculate OFDM subcarrier spacing, useful and cyclic-prefix symbol durations, symbol rate and occupied bandwidth from sample rate, FFT size and active subcarriers.
tools.method: For sample rate Fs in hertz and an N-point FFT, the sample period is 1/Fs, subcarrier spacing is Fs/N and the useful symbol duration is N/Fs. The cyclic prefix is the selected exact fraction of N samples and must resolve to a whole sample. Total symbol duration is (N + Ncp)/Fs, symbol rate is Fs/(N + Ncp), occupied bandwidth is the active-subcarrier count times Fs/N, and prefix overhead is Ncp/(N + Ncp). The occupied-bandwidth value is a nominal occupied-subcarrier span; guard bands, windowing, spectral masks and standard-specific fractional prefixes are not modelled.

tools.name: End Credits Roll Planner
tools.description: Plan end-credits timing from text rows, line height and frame size, with whole-frame durations, frame-aligned scroll speed and a copyable edit plan.
tools.method: Each text row, including a blank spacer row, occupies the supplied line height. Content height is row count times line height, and travel distance is content height plus one frame height so the first row starts below the frame and the last row clears its top. In speed mode, requested duration is travel distance divided by pixels per second. In duration mode, the requested duration is the supplied target. Duration is rounded to the nearest whole frame at the supplied frame rate, then the frame-aligned speed is travel distance divided by that rounded duration. Movement per frame is travel distance divided by frame count. No font metrics, wrapping, rendered video or drop-frame timecode are inferred.

tools.name: Chord Quality Ear Trainer
tools.description: Train your ear to recognise triads and seventh chords played together or broken, with configurable chord sets and a running accuracy and streak.
tools.method: Each question draws a chord quality from the selected fixed pool and a root from MIDI 48-60 (C3-C4), keeping every root-position voicing at or below MIDI 71 (B4). Triads offer major, minor, diminished and augmented; seventh chords offer dominant, major, minor, half-diminished and diminished; mixed combines all nine qualities. Chord tones use the recorded semitone offsets from the root and sound together, low to high or high to low. Frequencies use 12-tone equal temperament with A4 = 440 Hz: frequency = 440 x 2^((MIDI - 69)/12). A question does not immediately repeat the previous quality when another choice is available. Answers match the exact chord-quality identifier; accuracy is correct answers divided by questions asked, rounded to a whole percent. The Web Audio API synthesises every tone locally with a triangle-wave envelope; there are no audio files, microphone input, storage or network requests. This practises chord-quality recognition, not absolute pitch, inversion identification, harmonic function or intonation.

tools.name: Eye Diagram Explorer
tools.description: Turn a binary sequence into an NRZ waveform and overlaid eye diagram with rectangular or raised-cosine pulses, adjustable roll-off and sampling density.
tools.method: Map binary 0 and 1 to NRZ amplitudes -1 and +1. The rectangular pulse is one inside |t/T| < 1/2, half at its edges and zero outside. The raised-cosine pulse is sinc(t/T) cos(pi beta t/T) / (1 - (2 beta t/T)^2), with its removable singularities evaluated by their limits and a six-symbol truncation on either side. Sum the shifted pulses, then overlay two-symbol traces centered on each interior symbol's ideal sampling instant. Vertical opening is the lowest nonnegative center level minus the highest negative center level, or N/A when both polarities are not present. Noise, jitter and channel loss are excluded.

tools.name: Golf Stableford Scorecard
tools.description: Score an 18-hole Stableford round from par, stroke index, gross scores and playing handicap, with net scores and per-hole points.
tools.method: For each of exactly 18 holes, validate par 3-5, gross score 1-30 and a unique stroke index from 1 through 18. A nonnegative playing handicap h allocates floor(h/18) strokes to every hole plus one extra where stroke index is at most h mod 18; h may be 0 through 54. A plus handicap from -1 through -18 instead allocates one negative stroke on each hole whose stroke index is at most abs(h). Net score is gross score minus allocated strokes. Stableford points are max(0, 2 + par - net score), without an artificial upper cap. Totals and front/back-nine points are integer sums. The input must already be the applicable playing handicap; handicap allowances, unplayed holes and committee adjustments are outside the model.

tools.name: Video Transition Timeline Planner
tools.description: Calculate a video sequence's runtime and each clip's timeline edit points from clip durations and transition overlaps, using exact whole-frame arithmetic.
tools.method: Clip and transition durations accept decimal seconds, mm:ss or hh:mm:ss with at most three decimal places, from 0.001 through 86,400 seconds for clips and 0 through 86,400 seconds for transitions. The frame rate is 1-240 fps with at most three decimal places. Every duration is independently multiplied by the frame rate and rounded to the nearest whole frame; clips rounding below one frame are rejected. One transition is required per adjacent clip pair, with blank or zero rows representing straight cuts. Finished frame count is the sum of clip frames minus the sum of overlap frames. Each later clip starts at the previous clip's end minus their shared overlap. An overlap must be shorter than both adjacent clips, and a clip's incoming plus outgoing overlaps must be shorter than that clip, preventing non-monotonic or triple-overlap timelines. Up to 100 clips are supported. Labels are optional, whitespace-normalized and limited to 80 characters. Displayed times are derived from whole frames and rounded to milliseconds; this is not drop-frame SMPTE timecode, a transition renderer or a media inspector. Nothing is stored or transmitted.

tools.name: Map Tile Coordinate Calculator
tools.description: Convert WGS84 coordinates to Web Mercator XYZ map tiles and quadkeys, or decode a tile into its geographic bounds and center.
tools.method: Use the spherical Web Mercator XYZ tiling scheme at integer zooms 0 through 30. For a WGS84 latitude and longitude, with latitude limited to ±85.0511287798066 degrees and longitude to ±180 degrees, calculate x = floor((longitude + 180) / 360 × 2^zoom) and y = floor((1 − asinh(tan(latitude)) / π) / 2 × 2^zoom), using radians for the trigonometric operations. Clamp the positive 180-degree longitude and exact northern/southern limits to the final valid tile index. Reverse conversion uses longitude = x / 2^zoom × 360 − 180 and latitude = atan(sinh(π × (1 − 2y / 2^zoom))) for the northwest corner, with x + 1 and y + 1 giving the southeast corner and half-index offsets giving the center. The quadkey interleaves Y and X bits from most to least significant, with digit = xBit + 2 × yBit; zoom zero has an empty quadkey. Coordinate strings accept ordinary decimal notation with up to 13 fractional digits and no exponents. Tile indexes must be integers within the selected zoom's grid. Displayed coordinates are rounded to ten decimal places. This performs no datum transformation, routing, geocoding or map request, and nothing is stored or transmitted.
