tools.name: Dough Temperature Calculator
tools.description: Find the water temperature that brings a bread dough to a chosen finished temperature, counting the room, the flour, an optional preferment and the friction heat of mixing.
tools.method: The water temperature is the target dough temperature multiplied by the number of temperatures being averaged — 3 for a straight dough of water, flour and room, 4 when a preferment also counts — minus the flour temperature, the room temperature, the preferment temperature when used and the friction rise. The result is the water temperature that makes the mixed dough average out to the target, because the finished dough settles near the average of the temperatures that went into it. Every degree moved on the water moves the dough by one degree divided by the factor count, and cooler flour or a cooler room allows warmer water. The friction rise is the heat mixing itself adds and depends on the mixer type, the dough mass, the speeds and the mixing time, so it has to be measured for the equipment in use rather than assumed; published figures run from roughly 3 °C by hand to 13 °C on a planetary stand mixer. A required water temperature below 0 °C cannot be met with liquid water, so the flour must be chilled or part of the water replaced with ice. Values are refused outside 1 to 45 °C for the target, −20 to 50 °C for the flour, room and preferment temperatures and 0 to 30 °C for the friction rise, and decimal commas are accepted. The page does not estimate fermentation time, judge whether dough is proofed or make any food-safety claim, and it runs entirely in the browser with no storage, uploads or network access.

sources.title: The desired dough temperature formula multiplies the target by 3 for a straight dough or 4 when a preferment is used, then subtracts the flour, room, preferment and friction temperatures to give the required water temperature.

The friction factor is the temperature rise caused by mixing and varies with the mixer, dough mass, speed and mixing time; measured examples run from about 6–8 °F by hand to 22–24 °F on a planetary stand mixer.
The preferment version of the formula multiplies the desired dough temperature by four and subtracts the preferment temperature along with the room, flour and friction temperatures.

tools.name: Uplink Oversubscription Calculator
tools.description: Compare the combined bandwidth of a switch's access ports with the uplinks that carry it: oversubscription ratio, the load those uplinks see at peak, the headroom, and the uplink ports a target ratio needs.
tools.method: The oversubscription ratio is the combined line rate of the access ports divided by the combined line rate of the active uplink ports, both in the same unit and one direction: access capacity is the port count times the access port speed, uplink capacity is the active uplink count times the uplink port speed, and the ratio is the first divided by the second. Forty-eight 1 Gbps ports behind two 10 Gbps uplinks is 48 Gbps against 20 Gbps, or 2.4:1, which means the access ports cannot all send at full line rate through the uplinks at the same time. A ratio at or below 1:1 means the uplinks match or exceed the access capacity, so the boundary is not oversubscribed. The peak demand is the access capacity multiplied by the share of line rate expected at the busiest moment, the uplink load is that demand as a percentage of the uplink capacity, and the headroom is the uplink capacity minus the demand, so a negative headroom means the assumed peak cannot pass in one direction even though the design ratio looks normal. The uplink count a target ratio needs is the access capacity divided by the target ratio times the uplink speed, rounded up to a whole port, and the headroom against the target is the target ratio times the uplink capacity minus the access capacity. Only active, forwarding uplink members are counted: a standby or blocked bundle member adds no usable bandwidth. The ratio describes provisioned capacity, not measured throughput, queueing, latency, per-flow hashing or traffic that stays on the same switch, so it is a planning figure for one boundary rather than a design certification; common guidance allows roughly 20:1 at the access edge and about 4:1 at aggregation and core. Values are refused outside 1 to 4096 access ports, 1 to 256 uplink ports, 1% to 100% peak utilization and a 1:1 to 100:1 target, port speeds come from a fixed list of line rates, and decimal commas are accepted. The page runs entirely in the browser with no storage, uploads or network access.

sources.title: Oversubscription is expressed as the ratio of the bandwidth the access ports could demand to the bandwidth the uplink provides, so a 48-port 1 Gbps switch with one 10 Gbps uplink is 4.8:1.

Widely used planning guidance puts the access-to-distribution oversubscription ratio at no more than 20:1 and distribution-to-core at no more than 4:1, and advises monitoring uplink bandwidth before changing the ratio.

tools.name: Mercator Scale Factor Calculator
tools.description: Show how far a Mercator or Web Mercator map stretches at a chosen latitude: the point scale factor sec phi, the scale error, the area inflation, the local scale a nominal 1:N map reaches there and the latitude a target factor is reached.
tools.method: A Mercator map touches the globe along the equator, where its scale is exact, and stretches every other parallel to the same length as the equator. The parallel on the globe has radius R cos phi while the map draws it with radius R, so the point scale factor is k = 1 / cos phi = sec phi for the absolute latitude phi; because the projection is conformal the meridian scale factor is the same value, which is why angles and small shapes are preserved. The scale error is (k - 1) x 100 percent, the area scale factor is the product of the two equal scales, k squared, so a region at 60 degrees covers four times the map area of the same region on the equator. A 1:N map that is true at the equator reaches 1:(N / k) at that latitude, which the page reports rounded to a whole denominator. The Mercator northing is R ln(tan(45 degrees + phi / 2)) with R = 6378137 m, the sphere radius Web Mercator uses, which equals 0 at the equator and 20037.5 km at the Web Mercator latitude limit of 85.0511287798066 degrees; that limit follows from the square world of the XYZ tile scheme and is the range this page accepts, in both hemispheres. The latitude at which a target scale factor k is reached is arccos(1 / k), reported with a note when it falls beyond the Web Mercator limit. Values are refused outside the latitude limit, a nominal scale from 1:100 to 1:1000000000 and a target factor from 1.01 to 100, and decimal commas are accepted. The page reports the properties of the spherical Mercator only: it does not add the small ellipsoidal correction that keeps Web Mercator from being exactly conformal on WGS 84 coordinates, it assumes the tangent case with the equator as standard parallel rather than a secant Mercator, and it is not a replacement for a projection library. It runs entirely in the browser with no storage, uploads or network access.

sources.title: The Mercator parallel and meridian scale factors are equal and both equal sec phi, so the point scale factor is 1/cos phi: about 1.15 at 30 degrees, 1.41 at 45, 2 at 60, 5.76 at 80 and 11.5 at 85, with an area scale factor of sec squared phi.

Web Mercator is a spherical Mercator that uses the same formulas at every scale, keeps meridians evenly spaced, inflates areas with distance from the equator and is normally cropped near 85 degrees north and south.

tools.name: Partition Alignment Calculator
tools.description: Align a disk partition start and size to the 1 MiB convention, to 512- or 4096-byte sectors and to a RAID stripe: the aligned start LBA, the padding a chosen offset wastes, the aligned end that lets the next partition start cleanly, and whether a 512e drive would have to read-modify-write.
tools.method: The planned start and the partition size are read in MiB with up to six decimals (decimal comma accepted) and converted to whole bytes by rounding to the nearest byte; the start must be 0 to 1,000,000 MiB and the size 0.000001 to 1,000,000 MiB. The logical and physical sector sizes are limited to 512 and 4096 bytes. The alignment unit is 1 MiB on its own; when a RAID stripe is enabled it becomes the least common multiple of 1 MiB and chunk x data disks, so a 256 KiB chunk over 6 data disks (a 1.5 MiB stripe) needs a 3 MiB unit, and a unit above 1 GiB is refused. The aligned start is the first multiple of the unit at or after the planned start, computed as byte arithmetic with no division; the aligned end is the first multiple at or after start plus size, so the next partition also begins on a boundary. All byte offsets are safe integers, and the start and end LBA are the offsets divided by the logical sector size. The verdict reports a start that is not a whole logical sector, a start that is sector-aligned but not aligned to the physical sector (a 512e drive would read-modify-write), a start that needs padding, or a start that is already aligned. The reference table lists the unit required by five common chunk and disk layouts. The calculation runs entirely in the browser with no storage, uploads or network access.

sources.title: GNU Parted manual: modern partitioning tools default to an optimal MiB alignment for msdos and gpt labels and can warn when a partition start or end is not aligned.
mdadm(8): the chunk size and the number of data disks define the stripe width that RAID0, RAID5, RAID6 and RAID10 write as one unit.
Linux kernel block-layer documentation: a drive reports both a logical and a physical block size, and requests that do not cover whole physical sectors force read-modify-write on 512e media.

tools.name: Swing Ratio Calculator
tools.description: Convert a swing percentage into the long and short note lengths, the long-to-short ratio and the off-beat delay for eighth- or sixteenth-note pairs, with the first four onsets in milliseconds and beats.
tools.method: The swing amount p is read as a percentage of the pair span from 50 to 75 (decimal comma accepted), and the tempo as 20 to 400 BPM (decimal accepted). One beat lasts 60000 / BPM milliseconds; an eighth-note pair spans one beat and a sixteenth-note pair spans half a beat. The first note therefore lasts p% of the pair and the second lasts 100 - p%, the long-to-short ratio is p / (100 - p), and the off-beat shift is the second onset minus the straight midpoint, so 50% is 0 ms and 60% pushes the off-beat late by a tenth of the pair. Feel bands follow the standard swing classification: 1:1 straight at 50%, between 1:1 and 2:1 soft swing, 2:1 triplet swing at 66.67% within 0.05 percentage points (so the rounded 66.7 also reads as triplet), between 2:1 and 3:1 hard swing, and 3:1 dotted hard swing at 75%. The grid lists the first four pairs with onsets in milliseconds and in beats. Values are exact notation timing, not a model of human micro-timing, and everything runs in the browser with no storage, uploads or network access.

tools.name: Pillow Cover Calculator
tools.description: Turn a pillow insert size into an envelope-back cut list: the finished cover, the front panel and the two overlapping back panels with seam, hem and ease allowances, plus the fabric area and the length needed on 44-inch fabric.
tools.method: The finished cover is the insert plus the chosen ease on both sides, and every panel adds the seam allowance to all four cut edges. The back is two rectangles the full width of the front: their combined height covers the front height plus the overlap, and each panel adds the opening hem so the turned-under edge lands on the seam line. Total fabric is the front area plus both back panels, and the length on 44 in (112 cm) fabric stacks the front and the two back panels along one width, so it is the front height plus twice the back panel height. Inputs are inches or centimetres (decimal comma accepted), inserts 2-60 in (5-152 cm), ease 0-3 in, seam 0-2 in, overlap 1-10 in and hem 0-2 in. It warns when the overlap exceeds half the front height and when a panel is wider than the fabric. It does not allow for directional prints, nap, pattern matching, shrinkage or squaring the fabric, and it is a planning estimate rather than a guarantee against a particular insert squishiness.

tools.name: Antenna Downtilt Coverage Calculator
tools.description: Turn an antenna height, downtilt and half-power beamwidths into a ground coverage footprint: the near and far beam edges, the aim distance, the slant range and the path width at the aim point.
tools.method: Ground distance to a depression angle theta is h / tan(theta), with h in metres and theta in degrees. The beam centre uses the downtilt; the near edge uses the downtilt plus half the vertical beamwidth and the far edge uses the downtilt minus half of it, so there is no far ground edge when the upper half-power edge is at or above the horizon. The footprint is the far edge minus the near edge, the slant range is h / sin(theta), and the path width at the aim point is twice the centre distance times tan of half the horizontal beamwidth. The radio horizon is 4.12 x sqrt(h) km and is used only to flag a footprint that curvature would shorten. Inputs are metres or feet (decimal comma accepted), heights 1-300 m (3.3-984 ft), downtilt 1-45 degrees, vertical beamwidth 2-60 degrees and horizontal beamwidth 10-120 degrees. The model assumes flat ground with no terrain, structures or vegetation, a symmetric main beam, and no earth curvature in the footprint distances; it does not account for side lobes, antenna gain beyond the half-power width, or RF exposure limits.

tools.name: Billiards Cut Angle Calculator
tools.description: Measure the cut angle for a pool shot from the cue ball, object ball and pocket positions, with the ghost-ball aim point, contact point, cue and object travel and aim-line offset on 7, 8 or 9 ft tables in inches or centimetres.
tools.method: The cut angle follows from the line of centres. With cue ball C, object ball O and the selected pocket P, the unit vector u points from O to P, and the ghost-ball centre is G = O - 2r u, where r is the ball radius. The cue ball must travel from C to G, so the cut angle is the angle between C to G and u: it is 0 for a straight shot and approaches 90 degrees as the hit gets thinner. An angle above 90 degrees means C lies on the pocket side of O, so a centre-ball hit cannot send the object ball toward that pocket. The contact point on the object ball is O - r u, the cue-ball travel is the distance from C to G, the object-ball travel is the distance from O to P, and the aim-line offset from the object ball's centre is 2r sin(cut). Standard American pool balls are 2.25 in (57.15 mm) in diameter; the playing surfaces are 78 x 39 in (7 ft), 88 x 44 in (8 ft) and 100 x 50 in (9 ft). Coordinates run from the bottom-left corner with x along the long rail, in inches or centimetres, and every ball centre must sit at least one radius inside the cushions. The model assumes a centre-ball hit with no side spin, no throw, no cushion contact and no pocket-jaw effects, so it is a planning aid rather than a prediction that a shot drops.

tools.name: Rice Cooking Ratio Calculator
tools.description: Work out how much water and how big a pot a batch of rice needs and how many servings it makes, from the rice type, the dry cups, grams or cooked servings and an adjustable water-to-rice ratio.
aliases: How Much Water for Rice Calculator
how much water for rice calculator
tools.method: Water is quoted by volume against the dry rice, so the ratio is cups of water per cup of dry rice: the defaults are 1.75 for long-grain and medium-grain white rice, 1.5 for jasmine and basmati, 1.15 for short-grain sushi rice, 2.25 for brown rice, 3 for wild rice and 4.5 for arborio, and the field can be overridden to match a packet or a measured batch. A cup is 236.5882365 ml and the water in millilitres is the rice volume in cups multiplied by the ratio and by that figure. A gram amount is first turned into cups with the type's bulk density (185 g for long-grain, 180 g for jasmine and basmati, 190 g for medium-grain and brown, 200 g for short-grain and arborio, 160 g for wild rice), because the ratio applies to volume rather than mass. A serving is taken as half a cup of cooked rice, and a serving request is converted back into dry rice with the type's cooked expansion (3 cups cooked per cup dry for most white and brown rice, 2.7 for short-grain, 3.5 for wild), so the cooked volume and serving count are estimates of typical absorption rather than a measurement of the pan. The pot figure is simply the dry rice plus the water. Amounts are refused outside 0.05 to 40 cups, 10 to 6400 grams or 1 to 80 half-cup servings, and ratios outside 0.5 to 8; decimal commas are accepted. The page does not model soaking, evaporation, altitude, stirring or absorption differences between crops, and it makes no food-safety claim about cooking, cooling or storing rice. It runs entirely in the browser with no storage, uploads or network access.

sources.title: Wikipedia, Cooked rice: rice is generally cooked by absorption with roughly two parts water to one part rice by volume, and one cup of dry white rice yields about three cups cooked, though the exact figures depend on the variety.
Wikipedia, Brown rice: brown rice keeps its bran and germ, so it needs more water and a longer cooking time than white rice.
Wikipedia, Wild rice: wild rice is the grain of a North American water grass rather than a true rice, and the grains split open as they cook.
Wikipedia, Arborio rice: arborio is a short-grain Italian rice used for risotto, cooked by adding hot stock a ladle at a time rather than all at once.

tools.name: Structured Cabling Run Estimator
tools.description: Estimate how much Ethernet cable a set of data drops needs and how many boxes to order, from the drop count, the average run, riser distance, slack allowance and box size.
tools.method: Every drop is charged the average horizontal run plus the riser distance, and that figure is increased by the slack allowance: cable per drop = (average run + riser) x (1 + slack / 100). The job total is that figure multiplied by the number of drops, and the boxes to buy are the total divided by the box size rounded up to the next whole box, with a one-part-in-a-billion tolerance so a total that lands exactly on a full box is not rounded again. Box sizes are the international foot definition (0.3048 m), so the 1000 ft box is 304.8 m and the 500 ft box is 152.4 m, with a 500 m drum as the third choice; feet are reported as metres divided by 0.3048. Patch cords are counted separately as drops x patch cords per drop, because they are bought as assemblies rather than cut from the box. Inputs are refused outside 1 to 1000 drops, 0.5 to 150 m average run, 0 to 100 m riser, 0 to 50 percent slack and 0 to 4 patch cords per drop, drops and patch cords must be whole numbers, and decimal commas are accepted. The page does not survey a building, choose a cable category, check conduit or tray fill or bend radius, allow for waste from failed pulls, or know a manufacturer's actual box length; the average run and the slack allowance are site assumptions the user supplies. It runs entirely in the browser with no storage, uploads or network access.

sources.title: Wikipedia, Structured cabling: a structured cabling system runs horizontal cabling from each outlet to a telecommunications room, so a drop needs both a horizontal run and any riser distance to the room.
Wikipedia, Twisted pair: Ethernet cabling is sold on reels and in pull boxes in fixed lengths, which is why a job is ordered in whole boxes with slack for routing and termination.
Wikipedia, Foot (unit): since the 1959 international yard and pound agreement one foot is exactly 0.3048 metres, the conversion used for the 1000 ft and 500 ft box sizes.

tools.name: Map Fit-Bounds Zoom Calculator
tools.description: Find the Web Mercator zoom level that fits a latitude/longitude bounding box into a map viewport, with the box centre, screen span, ground resolution, map scale and tile range.
tools.method: Each edge is projected onto the spherical Web Mercator plane (EPSG:3857): x = (longitude + 180) / 360, and y = (1 - ln(tan(pi/4 + phi/2)) / pi) / 2, with phi the latitude in radians clamped to the +/-85.0511287798066 degree limit where the projection is finite. The box width is the eastward longitude difference divided by 360, taken through 180 degrees when west is larger than east, and the box height is the difference of the two y values. At zoom z the world is tile size x 2^z pixels across, so the box spans box width x tile x 2^z pixels horizontally and box height x tile x 2^z vertically. The exact fit zoom is the smaller of log2(viewport width / (box width x tile size)) and log2(viewport height / (box height x tile size)); that value is rounded down to a whole zoom, with a one-part-in-a-billion tolerance so an exact fit stays at its own zoom, and clamped to the usual 0 to 22 range. At the chosen zoom the page reports the box centre (the wrapped midpoint of the x range and the midpoint of the y range inverted back to latitude), the box size in screen pixels, the ground resolution at the centre 40075016.68557849 m x cos(centre latitude) / world width, the map scale denominator at 96 dpi (metres per pixel divided by 0.0254/96), and the tile columns and rows covering the box, with a one-part-in-a-billion tolerance so an edge that sits exactly on a tile boundary does not add an empty row or column. Inputs are refused outside -90 to 90 degrees latitude, -180 to 180 degrees longitude, a viewport of 1 to 10000 whole pixels and the 256 or 512 pixel tile sizes; north must be greater than south, west and east must differ, and a box that collapses to zero height after clamping is refused. Decimal commas are accepted. The page does not reproject to other datums or projections, report resolution anywhere but the box centre, know about terrain, tilt, padding, tile overlap or retina tile sets beyond the tile-size choice, and it does not fetch or draw any map. It runs entirely in the browser with no storage, uploads or network access.

sources.title: Wikipedia, Web Mercator projection: the spherical projection normalises longitude and a stretched latitude, and is only finite up to about 85.0511 degrees, the clamp this page applies.
OpenStreetMap Wiki, Slippy map tilenames: a zoom level z splits the world into 2^z by 2^z tiles of 256 pixels, so the world is 256 x 2^z pixels wide and a viewport fit follows from that ratio.
Wikipedia, Scale (map): map scale is a ratio of map distance to ground distance, computed here from the ground resolution at the box centre with 96 CSS pixels to the inch.

tools.name: Disk I/O Throughput & IOPS Calculator
tools.description: Turn sustained IOPS, block size and average latency into throughput in MB/s, data per hour and per day, time per I/O, the queue depth Little's law needs, and the IOPS a given queue depth can sustain.
tools.method: Every operation is assumed to move exactly the chosen block size, so the throughput is the sustained IOPS multiplied by that block size in bytes: 10,000 IOPS of 4 KiB is 40,960,000 bytes per second. Decimal units divide by 1,000,000 for MB/s and binary units by 1,048,576 for MiB/s; the data per hour is bytes per second x 3600 in decimal GB, the data per day is bytes per second x 86400 in decimal TB, and the time to move 1 TiB is 1,099,511,627,776 bytes divided by the byte rate in hours. The time per I/O is one second divided by the IOPS and is shown in microseconds. Little's law gives the average number of requests in flight as the completion rate times the average latency, so the queue depth needed is IOPS x latency in seconds (2 at 10,000 IOPS and 0.2 ms); when a queue depth is supplied, the IOPS that depth can sustain at the same latency is depth / latency, the headroom is that figure minus the entered rate, the utilization is the entered rate divided by that maximum, and an entered rate equal to the maximum is treated as covered. IOPS accepts 0.001 to 100,000,000, latency 0.001 to 60,000 ms, and the optional queue depth a whole number from 1 to 65,536; the nine block sizes run from 512 bytes to 1 MiB, decimal commas are accepted and exponent notation is refused. All arithmetic is double precision. The figures describe a steady state and do not model bursts, read/write mixes, sequential versus random placement, RAID write penalties, controller caches, filesystem overhead, thin provisioning or network storage, and the page does not benchmark, read or modify any device. It runs entirely in the browser with no storage, uploads or network access.

sources.title: Wikipedia, IOPS: the operation rate a storage device sustains and the block size each operation transfers together determine the byte throughput.
Wikipedia, Little's law: the long-run average number of items in a system equals the arrival rate multiplied by the average time each item spends there, which is the queue depth relation used here.
Linux kernel block-layer documentation: I/O requests are queued against a device queue with a bounded depth, so the queue depth and the per-request latency bound the achievable completion rate.
